text: Azure Firewall and AWS Network Firewall are both fully managed, stateful network firewalls sitting in front of an entire virtual network rather than one subnet or instance — but their rule models, and the way traffic actually gets routed into them, are built on different ideas worth knowing before you design either one.

Azure Firewall rules live in an Azure Firewall Policy, organized into rule collections with their own priority. Network rules filter by the classic five-tuple — source, destination, protocol, port — essentially an NSG rule centralized for a whole hub. Application rules filter by fully qualified domain name instead, so you can allow a domain like windowsupdate.com without tracking its changing IP ranges, which a network rule structurally cannot do. A third type, NAT rules, handles DNAT at the firewall's public IP.

AWS Network Firewall splits its rules differently: stateless rule groups do a fast first pass on the same five-tuple, each rule carrying an explicit priority and an action like pass, drop, or forward to the stateful engine. Stateful rule groups are where the real depth lives, written in Suricata-compatible syntax — the same rule language the open-source Suricata IDS and IPS engine uses. FQDN filtering isn't a separate rule type here; it's a Suricata rule using a keyword like tls.sni against the HOME_NET variable.

The wiring differs just as much as the rules. Azure Firewall is one regional instance living in its own AzureFirewallSubnet, reached because a user-defined route sends outbound traffic to its private IP as the next hop. AWS Network Firewall instead deploys a firewall endpoint into each Availability Zone you want covered, so every protected subnet's route table has to point at the endpoint in its own AZ — a real per-AZ wiring difference, not just a naming one.

Depth of inspection is gated differently too. Azure Firewall's Standard SKU covers network, application, and NAT rules plus threat-intelligence filtering, and you have to step up to Premium for TLS inspection, an IDPS engine, and URL filtering. AWS Network Firewall bundles that depth straight into its always-available stateful engine. Both support centralized, multi-account policy through their respective Firewall Managers.

A firewall still only filters what's exposed to it in the first place. The next lesson goes a step further — Azure Private Endpoint and AWS PrivateLink, which keep traffic to a managed service off the public internet entirely, instead of just filtering it once it arrives.
